## Overview

RLMGC01 addresses #409 D4: whether wave-1 verbal reasoning predicts the shape of the subsequent word-reading trajectory rather than only a single gain. The outcome is confirmed 90-item BAS word reading (`basread`); the baseline proxy is confirmed 21-item BAS Similarities (`bassim`). The primary panel is restricted to the three annual waves reported by Byrne, MacDonald and Buckley (2002).

The analysis retains children with wave-1 similarities observed and word reading observed at two or more of waves 1–3. Reading-group-specific nuisance intercepts and slopes absorb the very different average trajectories of the Down-syndrome, average-reader and reading-matched cohorts. The baseline-ability coefficients are shared across groups to avoid estimating three weakly informed associations. Child random intercepts account for stable repeated-measures dependence; the model deliberately omits 87 child-specific random slopes, which are weakly supported by one outcome over three waves. The four children without wave-1 similarities and children with fewer than two reading observations are excluded before fitting; remaining missing reading cells are masked rather than imputed.

## Model structure

For child $i$ in reading group $g$ at wave $t$, the latent word-reading logit is linear in standardised age $a_{it}$:

$$
\theta_{it} = \operatorname{intercept}_{i} + \operatorname{slope}_{i} a_{it}.
$$

The group-specific population trajectory is combined with standardised wave-1 BAS similarities $z(S_i)$:

$$
\operatorname{intercept}_{i} = \alpha_g + \delta z(S_i) + \sigma^0_g z^0_i,
\qquad
\operatorname{slope}_{i} = \beta_g + \gamma z(S_i).
$$

The headline `gamma` asks whether a 1-SD higher wave-1 similarities score is associated with a faster word-reading growth rate within reading group. `delta` is the association with reading level at the pooled mean age, not at study entry. Observed scores use a masked Beta-Binomial likelihood with group-specific concentration.

Nothing in this model is causal. The cohorts were not randomised, similarities is a noisy verbal-reasoning proxy rather than general ability itself, and the reading-matched group was selected on word-reading level. A common `gamma` also assumes the ability–growth association is sufficiently similar across groups; the available sample does not support estimating three separate slopes reliably.
